content: The studies reviewed provide detailed insights into the relationship between physical activity (PA) and bone health outcomes in children and adolescents. 1. Study Sources and Data Reporting: Data were derived from 20 unique samples, including studies from CHMS, EYHS, HELENA, IDEFICS, NHANES, QUALITY, and Viva la Familia cohorts. Results were reported separately, and participants were counted only once. Two studies used CHMS data (Colley et al., 2012; Janssen et al., 2013), 12 studies used EYHS data (e.g., Brage et al., 2004; Ekelund et al., 2006), five studies used HELENA data (e.g., Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2012), two studies used IDEFICS data (e.g., Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013b), eight studies used NHANES data (e.g., Mark and Janssen, 2008), three studies used QUALITY data (e.g., Henderson et al., 2012), and two studies used Viva la Familia data (e.g., Quiros-Tejeira et al., 2007). 2. Risk of Bias: Many studies exhibited a serious risk of bias due to pooled analysis across intervention and control groups without considering group effects (e.g., de Moraes et al., 2015). Missing data were prevalent, and insufficient information was provided to determine the proportion of missing data in several studies (e.g., Andersen et al., 2006; Rizzo et al., 2007). Detection bias was noted, as participants were retained if they provided PA data for at least 1–7 days, with PA levels slightly higher in those with fewer days of data (Owen et al., 2010). Selective reporting bias was observed, such as reporting systolic blood pressure without diastolic blood pressure (Hay et al., 2012). 3. Physical Activity Guidelines: The cut-point for meeting PA guidelines was defined as ≥60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) per day (e.g., Janssen et al., 2013; de Moraes et al., 2015). Some studies required ≥60 minutes of MVPA on at least 5 of 7 days (Mendoza et al., 2012). 4. Bone Health Outcomes: Bone health measures included bone mineral density (BMD), bone mineral content (BMC), cortical thickness, bone area, and strength indices. These were objectively measured using DXA or peripheral quantitative CT. Strong evidence indicates that children and adolescents who are more physically active have higher bone mass, improved bone structure, and greater bone strength (e.g., Gutin et al., 1999). 5. Associations Between PA and Bone Health: Total PA: Baseline total PA predicted follow-up BMC at the hip, trochanter, spine, and whole body in boys, and at the trochanter and whole body in girls (Janz et al., 2006). Total PA explained 1–2% of the variability in BMC. Vigorous Physical Activity (VPA): VPA was favorably associated with whole-body BMC (e.g., Tobias et al., 2007) and hip BMC (e.g., Janz et al., 2001). Mixed associations were observed for spine BMC and BMD, with favorable outcomes in girls but null results in boys (e.g., Janz et al., 2001). Moderate-to-Vigorous Physical Activity (MVPA): MVPA was associated with favorable hip BMC outcomes (e.g., Janz et al., 2008) but showed mixed results for spine BMC and BMD. Light Physical Activity (LPA): LPA showed null associations with whole-body BMC but favorable associations with upper and lower limb BMC (e.g., Tobias et al., 2007). 6. Bone Strength and Structural Measures: Total skeletal area and cortical bone area were favorably associated with PA (e.g., Janz et al., 2001; Sayers et al., 2011). Mixed associations were observed for femoral neck cross-sectional area and section modulus, with favorable outcomes in girls but null results in boys (e.g., Janz et al., 2004). 7. Quality of Evidence: The quality of evidence from cross-sectional studies was downgraded from low to very low due to serious risks of bias in 24 studies, reducing confidence in the observed effects. 8. Key Findings: Children and adolescents who engage in higher levels of PA, particularly MVPA and VPA, tend to have better bone health outcomes, including higher BMC and BMD, improved bone structure, and greater bone strength. The associations between PA and bone health outcomes vary by PA intensity, anatomical region, and sex, with some mixed or null findings. This detailed analysis underscores the importance of physical activity, particularly higher-intensity activities, in promoting bone health during childhood and adolescence. However, methodological limitations and biases in the reviewed studies highlight the need for more rigorous research to strengthen the evidence base.
